5 Reasons Plan 9 from Outer Space Is a Horror Movie Classic

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 16:12
Instaread
 Adam Page  November 12, 2026  Leave a Comment on 5 Reasons Plan 9 from Outer Space Is a Horror Movie Classic  Posted in Horror Movies
Share: XFacebookPinterestReddit

There are cinephiles out there who will tell you, with a totally straight face, that Citizen Kane is the greatest movie ever made. And that’s absolutely fine. It’s a perfectly respectable opinion held by perfectly respectable people, those who alphabetize their DVD collection and floss regularly.

Then there’s the rest of us. Those who know that somewhere in a cardboard-tombstoned graveyard, under a night sky made of black construction paper and hope, Ed Wood was making the real greatest movie of all time: 1957’s Plan 9 from Outer Space.

Plan 9 from Outer Space has often been called “the worst movie ever made” by people with no imagination or joy in their hearts. Those people are wrong. Plan 9 isn’t the worst movie ever made; it’s a horror classic and today I’m going to prove it, one glorious hubcap-shaped flying saucer at a time.

So, dim the lights and ignore the fact that the sun is clearly visible in a few “night” scenes as we count down the top five reasons this shambling and cheerfully undead piece of celluloid deserves its place in the horror pantheon next to Boris Karloff’s Frankenstein and Bela Lugosi’s Dracula. One of whom, incidentally, is actually in this movie! Well, sort of. Technically. In spirit in a way that will make sense in a moment but also never make sense.  

5. The Zombies Are Genuinely Unsettling

Let’s start with the monsters, because that’s what you go to a horror movie for.

Plan 9 from Outer Space doesn’t skimp on the monsters; but it does skimp on, let’s say, budget, competent lighting, a finished script, and the general laws of physics.

The premise for those who haven’t seen it (and really, bless you, savor that innocence): aliens from a far off planet are worried that humanity is on the verge of inventing a doomsday weapon called the “Solaronite” that could destroy the universe. So, they decide the best diplomatic solution isn’t a conversation or a treaty, not even a strongly worded letter, but “Plan 9” AKA raising the recently dead to stumble around a Southern California suburb and cause enough chaos that the governments of Earth will finally take alien visitors seriously.

This is, I should note, quite possibly the worst plan in the history of interstellar relations, ranking below “invade with lasers” and just above “leave a bad Yelp review.”

But the thing is, the zombies themselves and mainly Vampira gliding across the graveyard with her arms outstretched like she’s always reaching for a light switch she can’t quite find, and the shambling, cape-shrouded figure meant to be Bela Lugosi (it wasn’t, Lugosi died while filming so Ed Wood just stuck a cape in front of his chiropractor’s face) have an eerie and dreamlike quality that really can’t be sanded away. There’s something about the slow, silent, arms-first shuffle through a graveyard clearly made of cardboard headstones that taps into something primal. Less “competent zombie effect” and more “recurring nightmare you had as a child.” And, if you think about it, that’s actually a higher register of horror than most modern zombie movies manage with their huge budgets and foley-artist moans!

Vampira, especially, deserves her own paragraph and maybe her own wing in the Horror Hall of Fame. Malia Nurmi originated the black-clad, tiny-waisted horror hostess persona years before Elvira ever drew on eyeliner and her wordless performance here (she refused to say Ed Wood’s dialogue which is, frankly, fair enough) is really one of the most striking visual moments in 1950s low-budget horror. She seems to become a zombie, all sharp angles and hollow-eyed silence, and each time she appears on screen the movie momentarily achieves real dread before cutting back to two pilots in a cockpit arguing in front of what is very obviously a shower curtain.

This is the basic paradox of Plan 9 from Outer Space: it stumbles into moments of real horror craft by accident. You can’t plan that kind of beautiful disaster, you can only witness it.

4. Against All Odds, the Atmosphere is Somehow Perfectly Gothic

Every great horror movie needs atmosphere; shadows stretching across the moonlit lawn, fog rolling through a graveyard, the sense that something is deeply and cosmically wrong with the world… Plan 9 from Outer Space delivers all of this! Mainly because Ed Wood couldn’t afford to shoot his film any other way.

The graveyard set, reused and recycled across scenes with the happy confidence of a man who knows nobody’s checking the receipts, is a masterclass in make-do gothic minimalism. The tombstones wobble and the fog machine seems to have two settings: “none” and “the graveyard is now a sauna.” The day-for-night photography is so inconsistent that whole funeral processions seem to happen in a state of meteorological chaos, like even the sun can’t decide if it wants to take part in this movie…

But, like a miracle, none of this really undermines the horror atmosphere. It seems to enhance it. There’s a sickly, hallucinatory feeling to a graveyard that keeps changing lighting conditions mid-scene, like reality is glitching, or like you’ve wandered into a nightmare that hasn’t fully decided on its own internal logic. Modern horror directors spend millions on strange dream logic. Ed Wood did it with a few sheets of plywood and sheer audacity.

Then there’s the flying saucers. Models, dangling from visible strings and wobbling through scenes with all the aerodynamic grace of a paper plate thrown by a toddler having a tantrum. On paper, it’s the least scary thing imaginable. But in practice there’s something so wrong about those ships; the jerky and unnatural movements, how they hover with all the confidence of a drunk uncle at a wedding. They don’t move like anything in the natural world. Of course, they don’t move like decent special effects either. They’re in a strange third category of things moving in ways they shouldn’t be, and if you strip horror down to brass tacks, that’s kind of the whole point of the genre.

I love gothic horror, and it’s always been about atmosphere over logic; the sense of dread outweighs the sense of plausibility. Plan 9 from Outer Space achieves this ratio more completely than nearly any other movie in the genre’s history, purely by having no other choice.

3. Criswell’s Narration Is One of the Creepiest Things Ever Committed to Film

We have to talk about Criswell.

Criswell, real name Jeron Criswell King, was a self-proclaimed psychic who made a career predicting things that never happened with the unshakable confidence of a man who has never been held accountable for anything. He opens Plan 9 from Outer Space with a monologue so brilliantly unhinged that it deserves to be studied in film schools as an accidental masterclass in ominous delivery.

“Greetings, my friends,” he intones, dressed head to toe like a funeral director who’s had an espresso too many, staring directly into the camera with a fixed and unblinking gaze which makes me feel like he can really see my future (and is mildly disappointed in it). “We are all interested in the future, for that is where you and I are going to spend the rest of our lives.”

Read that sentence again and sit with it for a second. On its face, it’s one of the most banal statements ever recorded. Of course we’re all going to spend the rest of our lives in the future! By definition, that’s what the future is. But Criswell delivers it with such a grave and funereal certainty that it becomes chilling. He’s a man who has weaponized tautology, successfully becoming someone who could read you the ingredients off a cereal box and have you checking the locks on your doors at night.

Criswell’s narration bookends Plan 9 from Outer Space and pops up throughout the explain plot points the movie itself just doesn’t establish, and each time he appears, the temperature of the room drops three degrees. There’s a reason horror anthology shows like Tales from the Crypt or Creepshow rely on a ghoulish host to set the tone: the direct-address narrator, staring past the fourth wall into your real living room, is one of the horror genre’s oldest and most effective tricks. Criswell doesn’t do it through camp irony or winking self-awareness (that came later with Elvira and the Crypt Keeper) but through pure, deadly earnestness. He believes every word, and because he does, just for a second so do you.

By the time he delivers the movie’s legendary closing lines, asking us “Can you prove that it didn’t happen?” you’ve been narrated at by a man so committed to cosmic dread that Vincent Price himself would nod approvingly from whatever gothic manor he’s currently haunting.

2. It Embodied the “So Bad It’s Good” Horror Subgenre Before It Existed

This is where we start the legacy argument, because a real horror classic doesn’t just scare you in the moment, it changes the shape of the genre that follows. Plan 9 from Outer Space did exactly that, although not quite in the way Ed Wood intended.

Long before Tommy Wiseau’s The Room had audiences throwing plastic spoons at the screen, long before Troll 2 became a happy midnight-movie staple with its own documentary about its cult following, long before Neil Breen turned earnest incompetence into its own respected filmmaking tradition, there was Plan 9. Way back in 1957, Plan 9 was establishing the ground rules for a whole subgenre of horror-adjacent cinema: movies so sincerely wrong that the loop back around into something transcendent.

This matters more for horror than any other genre because horror has always had a more intimate relationship with camp and failure. Think about the over-the-top Universal monster sequels of the 1940s. The cheery gore-and-rubber theatrics of Herschell Gordon Lewis. The whole drive-in schlock system of the 1950s and ‘60s, when a double bill of Plan 9 from Outer Space and The Blob was just a good Tuesday night.

Horror fans always understood something that the prestige-cinema types never quite grasp: the line between “so scary it’s brilliant” and “so bad it’s brilliant” is quite a lot thinner and a lot more interesting than anyone wants to admit. Both need total, unguarded sincerity and both need a moviemaker who’s not protecting themselves with irony. The creative behind the madness is just going for it and to hell with the consequences and continuity errors!

Plan 9 from Outer Space planted the flag. It gave generations of horror-comedy hybrids, from Rocky Horror midnight screenings to the whole Troma back catalogue right up to Tim Burton’s loving 1994 biopic Ed Wood a template for how a movie can fail on every technical level and still succeed as an experience. You watch it like you’d gather around the campfire for a ghost story told by your weirdest uncle, the one who keeps forgetting which version of the story he’s telling while he’s holding up a paper plate and calling it a spaceship, and you still can’t look away from it for a second.

It’s not “bad horror.” It’s more like a new flavor of horror. One that took a few decades for the rest of the genre to catch up to.

1. It’s About Real, Cosmic Dread and It Means Every Word of It

Under all the jokes about wobbly tombstones, daytime-as-nighttime scenes, and all the other low-budget chaos: Plan 9 from Outer Space is really and sincerely a movie about existential horror on a cosmic scale. And it completely means it. With its whole cardboard heart.

If you strip away the production value (I know, there’s very little to strip, but stay with me) and look at the bones of the story: an advanced alien civilization is watching humanity from beyond the stars and has concluded our species is on the verge of unlocking a weapon that could destroy not just ourselves but the entire universe; every star and world, a chain reaction of destruction set off by our reckless ambition. They respond by raising our dead from their graves as a desperate and blunt-force warning. It may sound like a goofy premise but it’s the same worried, atomic-age dread that powered Godzilla, Invasion of the Body Snatchers, and The Day the Earth Stood Still — that fear that humanity’s own cleverness has become the monster and we’ve built something in our basements and labs that the universe itself can’t survive.

Ed wood wasn’t exactly a subtle moviemaker, or a competent one, or even one who understood how boom microphones are supposed to stay out of the shot. But he was sincere, and sincerity is the one ingredient that money and continuity can’t substitute for.

Every line of Criswell’s narration, each wobbling UFO, and each shambling zombie is offered up in unguarded earnestness. It’s a low-budget moviemaker really trying to tell something true and frightening about ourselves and using whatever materials he could on a shoestring budget in the last days of black-and-white B-movies. It’s that earnestness which is why the movie survives.

A movie that is trying with everything it has to unsettle you, even if its tools are a Halloween cape, a shower curtain, and a psychic in a cummerbund, will always out-live a movie that’s competently made and believes in nothing at all. 

Plan 9 from Outer Space believed. It believed in flying saucers made of hubcaps. It believed in zombies that could save the world by scaring it straight. And, most of all, it believed in the idea that a story told with absolute conviction can transcend every single limitation placed on it. And nearly 70 years later, we’re still watching and talking about it, still finding new things to say about a movie that’s supposed to be “the worst ever made.”

I think that’s the horror genre’s oldest and strangest sort of immortality: that one that doesn’t care how you got there, just as long as you never let go of the nightmare.

What’s YOUR Favorite Thing About the Horror CLASSIC Plan 9 from Outer Space…?

No list of Plan 9’s achievements would be complete without a tip of the hat to what I think is one of the best, strangest, and funniest continuity crimes: the moment where the gravediggers, after hearing a noise that’s “kinda spooky-like” and decide to leave, they start walking away from the grave they’ve been digging. Then they stop walking, for absolutely no reason, for about 13 seconds. They’re waiting for Vampira to make her entrance.

It’s not scary or atmospheric, but it’s a perfect distillation of what makes Plan 9 immortal. Even when it’s falling apart in front of you on camera, you can’t stop watching. And isn’t that the highest compliment you can pay a horror movie? That it got under your skin? Even if it took cardboard tombstones instead of a chainsaw?

So, long may Criswell’s cummerbund flap in the wind of cinema history. Long may the hubcap flying saucers spin. Plan 9 from Outer Space wasn’t about competent movie making; it was about belief and dread, and the sheer will to tell a scary story and it didn’t matter what you had lying around the garage to tell it with.

If you’ve never given Plan 9 a chance before now, give it a go. If you’ve already watched it, let me know what your favorite scene was in the comments.
